title: Common Crawl
summary: A free, open repository of web crawl data collected since 2007 — petabytes of pages that power C4, RefinedWeb, and many LLM pretraining corpora.
details: Common Crawl is a nonprofit foundation that crawls the public web every month and publishes the results as open data on Amazon S3. Each crawl contains billions of pages in WARC, WAT, and WET formats, typically several hundred terabytes per month. Because raw crawls are noisy, most LLM datasets (C4, RefinedWeb, FineWeb) are filtered derivatives of Common Crawl. The data respects robots.txt, and the foundation publishes a columnar index plus a URL index API so researchers can query captures without downloading petabytes. It is the closest thing the open world has to a public copy of the web.
size: Petabyte-scale; 250B+ pages across monthly crawls since 2007

demo.title: Query the Common Crawl URL index
demo.program:
import requests
idx = "https://index.commoncrawl.org/CC-MAIN-2026-04-index"
params = {"url": "example.com", "output": "json"}
r = requests.get(idx, params=params, timeout=30)
lines = r.text.strip().split("\n")
print("captures:", len(lines))
print("first:", lines[0][:160])

title: The Pile
summary: EleutherAI's 825 GiB open pretraining corpus — 22 diverse subsets from web, books, code, and academic text used to train open models like GPT-J.
details: The Pile was assembled by EleutherAI in 2020 as an open, well-documented pretraining corpus. It combines 22 subsets: web text (Pile-CC), books (Books3, BookCorpus2, Gutenberg), academic writing (arXiv, PubMed Central, PhilPapers), code (GitHub, StackExchange), and more, totaling about 825 GiB and roughly 300B tokens with the GPT-2 tokenizer. Every subset has documented provenance and licensing notes, which made The Pile the reference corpus for open LLM research and the training set for GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, and Pythia.

demo.title: Stream one Pile document
demo.program:
from datasets import load_dataset
ds = load_dataset("EleutherAI/pile", split="train", streaming=True)
row = next(iter(ds))
print("subset:", row["meta"]["pile_set_name"])
print("chars:", len(row["text"]))
print(row["text"][:200].replace("\n", " "))

title: RefinedWeb
summary: A 600B-token heavily filtered web dataset from the Technology Innovation Institute — the pretraining base of the Falcon model family.
details: RefinedWeb starts from Common Crawl and applies aggressive filtering and fuzzy deduplication to keep only high-quality documents, yielding about 600 billion tokens. It was built for the Falcon LLMs (Falcon-40B, Falcon-180B) and released publicly so others can reproduce that data pipeline. The accompanying MacroData Refinement pipeline documents each filtering stage — language identification, heuristic quality filters, and MinHash deduplication — making RefinedWeb both a dataset and a recipe for turning raw crawls into training-grade text.

demo.title: Estimate tokens per document
demo.program:
# RefinedWeb-style quality filter sketch on a local text file
import re
def quality_ok(text):
    words = text.split()
    if len(words) < 50: return False
    alpha = sum(w.isalpha() for w in words) / len(words)
    return alpha > 0.6 and len(set(words)) / len(words) > 0.3
sample = open('/etc/hostname').read() * 20
print("passes filter:", quality_ok(sample))

title: LAION-5B
summary: 5.85 billion image-text pairs scraped from Common Crawl — the open dataset behind Stable Diffusion and open CLIP models.
details: LAION-5B, released by the LAION nonprofit in 2022, pairs 5.85 billion web images with alt-text captions, filtered with CLIP similarity scores. Subsets include LAION-2B-en (English), LAION-2B-multi, and LAION-1B-nolang. It enabled Stable Diffusion, OpenCLIP, and a wave of open text-to-image research. The dataset ships as parquet metadata plus image URLs (images are fetched, not redistributed), with NSFW and watermark detectors run over the pairs. Later audits flagged CSAM contamination in subsets, leading to takedowns and re-releases — a cautionary tale about web-scale curation.

demo.title: Inspect LAION parquet metadata
demo.program:
import pandas as pd
url = ("https://huggingface.co/datasets/laion/laion2B-en/"
       "resolve/main/part-00000-9ad8bb56-...-c000.snappy.parquet")
# schema check on a tiny public sample instead of the full shard:
df = pd.DataFrame([{"TEXT": "a cat", "URL": "http://x/y.jpg",
                    "WIDTH": 512, "HEIGHT": 512,
                    "similarity": 0.31}])
print(df.dtypes)
print("rows passing CLIP>=0.28:", (df["similarity"] >= 0.28).sum())

title: COCO Captions
summary: 330K images each with 5 human captions — the classic benchmark for image captioning and vision-language evaluation.
details: The COCO (Common Objects in Context) caption set contains over 330,000 images annotated with five human-written captions each, plus object detection and segmentation labels. Released by Microsoft researchers, it became the standard training and evaluation set for image captioning, and its Karpathy splits are still the default for vision-language papers. Captions are released under CC-BY 4.0; images carry Flickr licenses. Modern multimodal models still report COCO captioning scores (CIDEr, SPICE) as a basic grounding check.

demo.title: Load COCO-style captions

title: LibriSpeech
summary: 1,000 hours of read English audiobooks with transcripts — the standard speech recognition benchmark.
details: LibriSpeech, derived from LibriVox audiobooks, provides about 1,000 hours of 16 kHz read English speech aligned with text, split into clean and noisy subsets plus train/dev/test partitions. Released through OpenSLR, it became the default ASR benchmark: models report word error rate (WER) on test-clean and test-other. Its fixed splits and permissive CC-BY 4.0 license made results comparable across a decade of papers, from DeepSpeech to wav2vec 2.0 and Whisper-era models.

demo.title: Compute WER the LibriSpeech way

title: The Stack
summary: BigCode's multi-terabyte source-code corpus with per-file license tracking — the training data for StarCoder.
details: The Stack collects source code from GitHub across 300+ programming languages: v1 holds 3.1 TB (6.4 TB in v2) with near-deduplication and, crucially, license metadata per file. The Stack v1 was filtered to permissive licenses for StarCoder; the opt-out mechanism let developers remove their repositories, setting a precedent for consent in code datasets. It ships as parquet with fields for repository, path, language, and license, and remains the largest openly documented code corpus for training code LLMs.
license: Per-file (ODC-By for collection; StarCoder used permissive subset)

demo.title: Filter a code sample by license
demo.program:
allowed = {"mit", "apache-2.0", "bsd-3-clause", "isc"}
files = [
    {"path": "a.py", "license": "mit"},
    {"path": "b.py", "license": "gpl-3.0"},
    {"path": "c.js", "license": "apache-2.0"}]
kept = [f for f in files if f["license"] in allowed]
print("kept:", [f["path"] for f in kept])

title: RedPajama
summary: Together AI's 1.2T-token open reproduction of the LLaMA training mix — fully documented and Apache 2.0.
details: RedPajama-Data-1T replicates the data mixture described in the LLaMA paper using only openly available sources: Common Crawl derivatives, C4, GitHub, Wikipedia, books, arXiv, and StackExchange, totaling about 1.2 trillion tokens. Released under Apache 2.0, it let the open community train LLaMA-class models (the RedPajama-INCITE models) on a known mixture. Its data recipes and quality-filter code are public, making it a practical template for building a large pretraining mix without proprietary data.

demo.title: Reproduce a LLaMA-style data mixture

title: C4
summary: The 750 GB cleaned Common Crawl corpus built for T5 — one of the most reused English pretraining sets.
details: C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus) applies heuristic cleaning to Common Crawl: English detection, deduplication, removal of boilerplate, and filtering of offensive or low-quality text. Built by Google researchers for T5, the 750 GB English corpus became a default pretraining ingredient (used in LaMDA, LLaMA-era mixes) and the basis for many derivatives. Its cleaning script is public, so the same pipeline can be re-applied to newer crawls — the pattern behind most 'clean web text' datasets.
size: 750 GB English (original); multilingual mC4 extends it

demo.title: C4-style cleaning sketch
demo.program:
import re
def c4_clean(text):
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    if len(text.split()) < 5: return None
    if "lorem ipsum" in text.lower(): return None
    if text.count("{") > 2: return None  # drop code-heavy pages
    return text
print(c4_clean("Hello   world. This is a clean sentence about datasets."))

title: OSCAR
summary: A massive multilingual corpus built from Common Crawl — 150+ languages with per-language shards.
details: OSCAR (Open Super-large Crawled Aggregated coRpus) processes Common Crawl dumps into monolingual shards for more than 150 languages, with deduplication and language identification per document. Maintained by INRIA-affiliated researchers, it is the go-to open resource for multilingual pretraining when English-centric corpora fall short. Each language shard is distributed separately, and the pipeline (Ungoliant) is open source, so new crawls can be turned into fresh multilingual corpora on demand.

demo.title: Pick a language shard
demo.program:
shards = {"en": "2.3TB", "fr": "310GB", "sw": "4.1GB", "yo": "900MB"}
lang = "sw"
print(f"OSCAR shard for {lang}: {shards.get(lang, 'missing')}")
low = [l for l, s in shards.items() if "MB" in s]
print("low-resource shards:", low)

title: OpenWebText
summary: An open 38 GB replica of the WebText corpus behind GPT-2, built from highly-upvoted Reddit links.
details: OpenWebText replicates OpenAI's WebText methodology: scrape outbound links from Reddit submissions with a score of 3 or more, extract article text, and deduplicate. The result is about 38 GB of English web documents that approximate GPT-2's training distribution. Because WebText itself was never released, OpenWebText became the community's stand-in for GPT-2-era replication work and a popular fine-tuning corpus for smaller models.

demo.title: Deduplicate scraped docs (MinHash sketch)

title: SQuAD 2.0
summary: 150K reading-comprehension questions including unanswerable ones — the QA benchmark that defined an era.
details: The Stanford Question Answering Dataset pairs Wikipedia paragraphs with crowd-written questions; SQuAD 2.0 adds 50K unanswerable questions, forcing models to abstain when the text lacks the answer. Models are scored with exact match and F1 against human answers. Released under CC-BY-SA 4.0, SQuAD drove the BERT-era leaderboard race and remains a standard fine-tuning set for extractive QA and a sanity check for instruction-tuned models.

demo.title: Score an extractive QA prediction (F1)
demo.program:
def qa_f1(pred, gold):
    pt, gt = pred.split(), gold.split()
    common = sum((pt.count(w) for w in set(gt) if w in pt))
    if common == 0: return 0.0
    p, r = common/len(pt), common/len(gt)
    return 2*p*r/(p+r)
print("F1:", round(qa_f1("the capital is Paris", "Paris is the capital"), 3))

title: ImageNet-1K
summary: 1.28M labeled images across 1,000 classes — the dataset that launched the deep learning revolution.
details: ImageNet-1K contains 1.28 million training images organized into 1,000 object categories, with 50K validation images. The 2012 AlexNet win on the ILSVRC challenge proved deep convolutional networks at scale and kicked off the modern AI boom. Beyond classification, ImageNet-pretrained weights became the default visual backbone for transfer learning for a decade. Access is gated by research-only terms, and the full 21K-class version is rarely distributed now.

demo.title: Top-1 accuracy on toy predictions
demo.program:
preds = [3, 7, 7, 1]; labels = [3, 7, 2, 1]
top1 = sum(p == l for p, l in zip(preds, labels)) / len(labels)
print("top-1:", top1)

title: MS MARCO
summary: A million real Bing queries with 8.8M passages — the standard for neural search and retrieval training.
details: MS MARCO (Microsoft MAchine Reading COmprehension) released 1 million anonymized Bing queries paired with retrieved passages and human-judged answers. The passage-ranking split (8.8M passages) became the default training set for dense retrievers and rerankers, with a public leaderboard tracking MRR@10. Released for research use, it underpins modern retrieval-augmented generation: most open RAG pipelines train or evaluate their retriever on MS MARCO.

demo.title: MRR@10 for a ranked list

title: WIT
summary: 37.6M image-text pairs mined from Wikipedia across 108 languages — multilingual vision-language at scale.
details: WIT (Wikipedia-based Image Text) extracts 37.6 million image-text pairs from Wikipedia articles in 108 languages, using captions, alt text, and surrounding article context as the text side. Released by Google under CC-BY-SA, it is one of the largest multilingual multimodal datasets and a key pretraining source for multilingual CLIP-style models. Because Wikipedia text is curated, WIT pairs are cleaner on average than raw alt-text scrapes.

demo.title: Language coverage check

title: AudioSet
summary: 2.1M ten-second YouTube clips labeled with 527 sound classes — the ImageNet of audio.
details: AudioSet, released by Google, contains over 2 million 10-second clips from YouTube annotated with 527 sound-event labels (speech, music, sirens, dog barks). The audio itself is not redistributed — researchers fetch features or clips via provided tooling — but the ontology and labels are open. It is the standard pretraining and evaluation set for audio classification, sound-event detection, and audio embeddings, analogous to what ImageNet did for vision.
license: CC variants (labels open; clips via YouTube)

demo.title: Multi-label mAP sketch
demo.program:
import numpy as np
y_true = np.array([[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0]])
scores = np.array([[0.9, 0.1, 0.8], [0.2, 0.7, 0.3]])
aps = []
for c in range(3):
    order = np.argsort(-scores[:, c])
    prec = np.cumsum(y_true[order, c]) / np.arange(1, 3)
    aps.append(float(np.mean(prec[y_true[order, c] == 1])))
print("mAP:", round(float(np.mean(aps)), 3))

title: GigaSpeech
summary: 10,000 hours of transcribed English speech from audiobooks, podcasts, and YouTube — Apache 2.0.
details: GigaSpeech collects 10,000 hours of English speech from audiobooks, podcasts, and YouTube with automatic and human-verified transcripts, released under Apache 2.0 by SpeechColab. Subsets are labeled by source quality (XL down to XS/DEV/TEST), and the corpus includes punctuation and casing, unlike older ASR sets. Its permissive license and scale made it a favorite for training open Whisper-class models.

demo.title: Subset hour accounting

title: FineWeb
summary: Hugging Face's 15T-token filtered web corpus — the open data behind many 2024-era LLMs.
details: FineWeb applies large-scale filtering and deduplication to 96 Common Crawl snapshots, producing 15 trillion tokens of high-quality English web text (plus FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3T-token educational subset). The filtering pipeline — language ID, heuristic filters, MinHash dedup — is fully open, and ablations showed the data outperforming C4 and RefinedWeb on downstream benchmarks. It is the default open pretraining corpus for the post-2024 open-model wave.

demo.title: Deduplicate with a Bloom-style set
demo.program:
seen = set()
def dedup(doc):
    h = hash(doc)
    if h in seen: return None
    seen.add(h); return doc
docs = ["hello world", "hello world", "new text here"]
print([d for d in map(dedup, docs) if d])

title: Dolma
summary: AI2's 3T-token open corpus with a transparent license (ImpACT) — pretraining data for OLMo.
details: Dolma powers AI2's OLMo models: 3 trillion tokens from web, code, books, and academic sources with per-source documentation. Its ImpACT license family was designed for AI training data, spelling out allowed uses. Every OLMo release pairs model weights with the exact Dolma mixture and training code, making it the gold standard for fully reproducible LLM training.

demo.title: Mixture weight sanity check

title: SlimPajama
summary: A 627B-token aggressively deduplicated RedPajama — cleaner tokens, same Apache 2.0 license.
details: SlimPajama reprocesses RedPajama with stricter global deduplication (both exact and fuzzy), cutting it to 627 billion high-quality tokens. Built by Cerebras with Together AI, it demonstrated that dedup alone measurably improves downstream accuracy at fixed compute. The corpus and dedup code are Apache 2.0, making SlimPajama a drop-in cleaner substitute for RedPajama in open training runs.

demo.title: Fuzzy dedup with MinHash bands
demo.program:
import hashlib
def minhash(text, n=64):
    return sorted(hashlib.md5((text + str(i)).encode()).hexdigest()
                  for i in range(n))[:n]
a = minhash("the cat sat on the mat")
b = minhash("the cat sat on the mat!")
overlap = len(set(a) & set(b)) / len(a)
print(f"signature overlap: {overlap:.2f} -> {'dup' if overlap > 0.8 else 'keep'}")

title: OpenHermes 2.5
summary: Teknium's 1M-pair instruction dataset — mostly synthetic, Apache 2.0, a staple for open chat fine-tuning.
details: OpenHermes 2.5 aggregates about a million instruction-response pairs, heavily synthetic (GPT-4-generated) plus curated open sources, all normalized into ShareGPT/ChatML format. Released by Teknium under Apache 2.0, it became the default SFT mix for open chat models in the Nous-Hermes lineage. Its value is curation: diverse tasks, filtered quality, and a permissive license in one download.

demo.title: ChatML formatting for SFT
demo.program:
def to_chatml(instruction, response):
    return (f"<|im_start|>user\n{instruction}<|im_end|>\n"
            f"<|im_start|>assistant\n{response}<|im_end|>")
print(to_chatml("What is 2+2?", "2+2 equals 4."))

title: BookCorpus
summary: 11,000 unpublished books — the narrative-text corpus behind early sentence embeddings.
details: BookCorpus scraped 11,038 free unpublished books (romance, fantasy, sci-fi) from Smashwords, giving models long-form narrative text with consistent characters and plot. Though small by modern standards, it trained skip-thought vectors and early BERT-adjacent research, and its 'books' slice persists in The Pile as BookCorpus2. Distribution is research-use; the original site is defunct, so corpus copies circulate via academic mirrors.

demo.title: Long-document chunking for training

title: MMLU
summary: 15,908 multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects — the broad knowledge benchmark for LLMs.
details: MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) tests models on 57 subjects from elementary math to professional law, in 4-option multiple-choice format. Released by Berkeley researchers under MIT license, it became the headline number in every LLM release from GPT-4 onward. Scores are reported per-subject and averaged; 5-shot prompting is the standard protocol. Its saturation at the top end is driving harder successors, but MMLU remains the common yardstick.

demo.title: Score a 5-shot MMLU-style run
demo.program:
answers = ["A", "C", "B", "D", "A"]; gold = ["A", "B", "B", "D", "A"]
acc = sum(a == g for a, g in zip(answers, gold)) / len(gold)
print(f"accuracy: {acc:.0%}")

title: HumanEval
summary: 164 hand-written Python problems — the standard test of LLM code generation.
details: HumanEval, released by OpenAI with the Codex paper, contains 164 function-synthesis problems, each with a docstring prompt, reference solution, and hidden unit tests. The metric is pass@k: the fraction of problems solved within k samples. Under the MIT license, it became the default code benchmark, spawning HumanEval+ (more tests) and multilingual variants like HumanEval-X.

demo.title: pass@k estimation

title: Alpaca 52K
summary: Stanford's 52K GPT-3-generated instruction pairs — the dataset that democratized instruction tuning.
details: Self-Instruct-generated with text-davinci-003, Alpaca's 52,000 instruction-response pairs showed that a 7B LLaMA fine-tuned on them could follow instructions surprisingly well. Released under CC-BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial, inherited from the generator's terms), it sparked the open instruction-tuning wave: thousands of derivative datasets copy its format. Small, cheap, and historically pivotal.

for p in pairs:
